EPILOGUE

Alan Barnett Ph.D. and S. Katz Ph.D.

S. Katz

S. Katz  

Introduction

The vast agreement and synthesis of psychoanalytic thought about and on the use of metaphor expressed in this issue indicate paths open for further exploration. Most important, a clear consensus on the conceptual model of unconscious metaphor is formulated from a broad interdisciplinary base, one that is compatible with a functionally unified view of memory and inherently communicable emotion from modern neuroscience. Because this model both fits the observations of the psychoanalytic situation and conforms to biological knowledge, it represents a potentially incremental contribution to metapsychological theorizing that, eventually, may yield a better understanding of why particular analytic principles and techniques are valid and effective. Thus, the notion of an unconscious metaphoric process may be productive in elucidating many areas of psychoanalytic theory and practice (e.g., Barnett, 2007, 2008a, 2008b; Katz, in press/in preparation), proving this concept robust in progressive research. In this connection—and given the crucial importance of the ability of the analyst to discern, process, and play with metaphor as an essential aspect of treatment—it may be that consideration toward integrating this model into analytic training is called for in the near future, entailing curricular development at a basic level.

Our twin issues of Psychoanalytic Inquiry, “Exploring Emotional Memory—Psychoanalytic Perspectives” and “Metaphoric Processes in Psychoanalytic Treatment,” have pursued the basic psychoanalytic principle that what is of significance, value, or meaning for individuals, especially in relation to others, ultimately may be traced to memory—the memory of feelings. If our emotions, feelings, and their associated defensive patterns are also the original sources of metaphor as a way of understanding ourselves, others, and the objective world, then in accordance with Arnold Modell's eloquent epistemic argument in Imagination and the Meaningful Brain, a pluralistic, not reductionistic, approach to the study of mind is called for that includes psychoanalytic introspection and empathy (first and second person knowledge) in combination with an objective (third person) perspective.

PROLOGUE

Moisy Shopper M.D. and Linda Gunsberg Ph.D.

Linda Gunsberg

Linda Gunsberg  

Introduction

Psychoanalytically trained analysts and therapists who enter the Court as expert witnesses are often asked, “Why we have voluntarily chosen to do this?” Most of our colleagues assiduously avoid involvement in legal matters. Why do we enter into an arena where the venue and rules are so different from, and even antithetical to, our orientation and training? Why, when we are so accustomed to asking the questions, do we put ourselves in the position of being asked questions? Why do we expose ourselves to being devalued and have our weaknesses, insecurities, and foibles put on view by a well-trained cross-examiner? Why do we, who are accustomed to the intimacy, privacy, and confidentiality of our consulting rooms, abandon all that for the exposure to public and often media scrutiny? Whatever the reasons, there are a few psychoanalysts who choose to do this work and, hard as it may be, derive a sense of professional satisfaction from doing something challenging, exciting, and socially and psychoanalytically useful, and which by the very nature of the work involves a fascinating degree of continued learning.

If psychoanalysis is to be more than an expensive and time-consuming treatment for the few, it has to show its unique usefulness and application to understanding and clarifying issues in other fields. Although Freud's forays into legal issues were significant, they remained tangential to his main emphasis. Anna Freud's collaboration with Goldstein and Solnit (1973, 1979, 1986) directly applied psychoanalytic concepts to legal matters and specifically to the underlying presumptions the law makes about child custody issues and the child's developmental needs.

In many ways, the law and psychoanalytic thinking deal with identical issues but since there are different goals, these two fields have developed different methods, guiding principles, and professional heritage. Yet, they both have a strong investment in ascertaining the truth, in understanding motivations of individuals, in reconstructing the past (crime scene vs. child and adolescent past) in assessing emotional damages of traumatic events, in understanding a person's sexual behavior, and creating and establishing the best circumstances for children's emotional and intellectual growth. Depending on one's knowledge of these two fields, there are many other basic commonalities, where the law needs and often requires input from the mental health field to arrive at a judicious decision. It is the opinion of the two co-editors of this issue that psychoanalytic knowledge and training add a degree of expertise that we believe is not only important to forensic thinking and evaluations, but in certain instances, provides an understanding that is of higher quality than ordinarily available.

Interlude: Emotional Reactions to Forensic Work

Moisy Shopper M.D. and Linda Gunsberg Ph.D.

Linda Gunsberg

Linda Gunsberg  

Introduction

Dr. Alexander-Guerra offers an uninhibited account of the conflicting emotions and inner dialogue she faces when accepting and working on a forensic case. This dialogue brings the patient, the crime committed, the Court, the attorneys, and Dr. Alexandra-Guerra's own family prominently into the foreground. Dr. Alexander-Guerra delineates the conflicts encountered into ethical, clinical, and personal. Although her forensic work is primarily that of treating the forensic patient, her contributions can be applied also to the forensic evaluation of an individual.

Dr. Alexander-Guerra reminds us that, although psychoanalysts have not usually committed murders, we do recognize and feel within ourselves fantasies and wishes to murder. Being at the other end of this continuum can be both a relief to the psychoanalytic forensic expert and psychoanalysts and engender great anxiety, in that “there but for the grace of God go I.”

In addition, Dr. Alexander-Guerra grapples with the interesting issue of different fee schedules for forensic versus customary psychoanalytic work. She resolves this issue for herself by charging the same fees for both works, to avoid the lure of forensic work because of the higher fee (and headaches) often associated with it.

Interlude: Voices for Psychologically Injured Children: Psychoanalytic Testimony During Civil Litigations Helps Bring Social Change, Settlement, and Jury Awards

Moisy Shopper M.D. and Linda Gunsberg Ph.D.

Linda Gunsberg

Linda Gunsberg  

Introduction

Dr. Kliman presents us with a detailed assemblage of cases, which not only had a profound effect on social policy, but also gives evidence of his unabashed dedication to psychoanalytic thinking and conceptualization. Within the context of a detailed presentation of normal development, Kliman was able to convincingly show how multiple traumata adversely damaged the children on whose behalf he testified. Given the lengthy time that litigation involves, Kliman decided to videotape his interviews with the children. This not only created a permanent record, but also allowed the Court to see how information was obtained. This is particularly important in these times of suggestive and coerced questioning of young children. The videotape not only preserves the memory of events, but offers the affective component, an advantage since the plaintiff child may be called to testify several years after the event when memory condensations, fading, and amnesia tend to distort recall, thus raising issues of child credibility where there should be none. Videotaping over time allowed Kliman to document the long-term effects of the traumata (the psychological deterioration over time) and to make available to the Court the natural history of post-traumatic stress disorder.

Kliman is also very clear about the need for cooperation, consultation, and mutual education between the psychoanalytic expert and the retaining attorney. Although seldom stated directly, a well-prepared knowledgeable psychoanalytic expert educates the attorney in the utility and necessity of a psychoanalytic approach. Using his analytically honed skills, Kliman was able to successfully ascertain unethical behavior of the opposing defense attorney.

Although monetary reward provides some measure of the degree to which the jury is swayed, it does more than that. It shows institutions and our society how vulnerable children are to trauma, to the absence of parental ministrations, and to the shortcomings of our institutions who purport to care for children.

Interlude: Like Father, Like Son: A Psychoanalytical Approach to Interviewing in Extreme Circumstances

Moisy Shopper M.D. and Linda Gunsberg Ph.D.

Linda Gunsberg

Linda Gunsberg  

Introduction

Although the penal system is not known for fostering a psychoanalytic approach to the prison and its inmates, more and more analysts are involving themselves in evaluating and advising in forensic matters and other areas where the mental health of individuals is severely stressed. Judging by the paucity of analysts involved in these legal and penal areas, many may deem themselves either unsuited or uninterested in leaving the confines of their consulting room. However, psychoanalysts may be quite ignorant of the opportunities and challenges of forensic and penal consultation. In the following article, one budding analyst comes to the field in the most common and natural way, that is, following in the footsteps of his father. Howard Osofsky has developed a long-standing and mutually respectful relationship with the warden and staff of the Angola Louisiana State Penitentiary, often called “The Farm” by the inmates. “The Farm” also served as the nickname of Stanford University, where Michael Osofsky was a student.

With both police departments and prisons, there is a huge power differential between those in authority and those who come under the authority of police and prison guards. This power differential is a necessary prerequisite for abuse of inmates. Prevention of abuse resides not so much with the “kindness” of staff as with their discipline and training, and the attitude and atmosphere created by their administrative superiors, namely the warden and his/her assistants. Although prison guards, in general, can be said to be working in an “extreme” environment, “extreme” is even greater with guards assigned to death row and designated to participate in the execution of an inmate. Osofsky and Osofsky have found that, despite the stress, or as a way to deal with the stress, the guards have developed a high degree of professionalism and humaneness, a finding counter to the expectations of many and contrary to earlier research in this area.

In this article, we are given a vignette of an adoring intelligent son researching what his father's profession is all about. As he learns, he becomes not only impressed but more knowledgeable and mature. To be given a small window into this process is an added dimension to this article.

EPILOGUE

Moisy Shopper M.D. and Linda Gunsberg Ph.D.

Linda Gunsberg

Linda Gunsberg  

Introduction

We realize that six special articles reflect a small representative interface that exists between psychoanalysis and the law. On first thought, many would think that these two disciplines, which are based on very fundamentally different concepts, are essentially antithetical. Law strives to remove affect and emotional factors to insure both a more cognitive approach to fact-finding and a more accurate and factual evaluation of contradictory evidence. In fact, the more passionate the nature of the crime/conflict and ensuing Court proceedings, the more the law strives to reduce emotional bias through recourse to changes in venue, careful screening of jurors and limiting the nature and form of questioning of witnesses. Certain evidence that may be prejudicial (such as the past sexual behavior of a rape victim claimant) is often excluded. Nevertheless passion, bias, vengefulness, compassion, and other feelings find their way into courtroom proceedings. Lawyers often become emotional in their questioning of witnesses and in their closing arguments. Every trial attorney is interested in selecting a jury favorable to his or her point of view and often will employ psychological experts to help identify those qualities and characteristics in prospective jurors favorable to their client (the jury selection process).

There are many other areas of collaboration between the attorney and a knowledgeable psychological expert. The psychological strategy of the overall case or the approach to the cross-examination of a witness is a frequent area requiring joint expertise. Opportunities for collaboration are often present even in legal conflicts that never go to trial. (Nevertheless, sometimes an attorney is too inexperienced in psychological issues to even know where and when help and consultation is useful.) However, with the decision to work together, opportunities present themselves much as they do in a psychoanalytic session: unexpected, or vaguely hinted at, yet vitally important.

Tractatus Metaphorico-Psychoanalyticus (with apologies to L.W.)

Lawrence Friedman M.D.

Lawrence Friedman

Lawrence Friedman  

Introduction

1. In the broadest sense, all nontautological predication [every act of describing, asserting, etc.]—indeed all communication—is metaphoric, inasmuch as it identifies some particular item with something else. Of course, there is a grammatical (and psychological) difference between attributing a general property to a general class (“Roses are red”), attributing a general property to an individual (“This rose is red”), comparing an individual to another individual (“My love is like a red, red rose”), and identifying an individual with another individual (“I am a rose of Sharon”). But in each case, we are asked to look at something in the light of something else, finding a certain abstraction in a specific individual or individuals. In the first three instances, we are made aware of our abstracting, which therefore has a certain precision; in the fourth instance (metaphor, strictu sensu) we must refocus without attending to—and thereby disciplining—our act of abstracting. It is the unconsciousness and indeterminateness of this sort of refocusing that gives ordinary metaphors their special power. (I will ignore metonymy and synecdoche as sharing the specificity of ordinary predication.)

1.1. All predication is thus propaganda, urging the receiver to see “this” as a “that.”

1.1.1. If it is easy to see “this” as a “that,” i.e., if it does not disturb other ways of seeing “this,” we take it as a simple true/false statement. In that case, only gentle propaganda is involved. (See Kenneth Burke [1954]. But also, of course, pre-Socratic philosophers, classical rhetoricians, Nietzsche [in Mandelbaum, 1971, p. 344], Foucault, 1972; White, 1973; and many others.)

1.1.2. If a predication grossly disturbs other ways of seeing something, it will be received as an error, or as a colorful, or inapt, or pretentious simile, or else as a metaphor. In any case, if it disturbs a customary way of seeing things, it will constitute strenuous propaganda.

1.2.3. Nothing is a metaphor. A statement can only be intended or accepted as a metaphor. The propaganda can be inadvertent, or intended; successful or unsuccessful.

PROLOGUE

Alan Barnett Ph.D. and S. Katz Ph.D.

S. Katz

S. Katz  

Introduction

In our prior issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry (Barnett and Katz, 2005), metaphoric processes emerged as a salient clinical factor when exploring ineffable aspects of transference. The contributors to that issue, representing diverse analytic perspectives, indicated collectively that metaphor, in fact, suffuses all facets of analytic investigation, and provides a possible theoretical base for interacting features of treatment (the intrapsychic and the intersubjective), as well as change. The potential synthesis of analytic perspectives around the ingredient of metaphor suggested that close attention to its workings in treatment could clarify and advance theories of psychoanalytic practice, expanding the common ground among them. This sequel is intended to pursue that conception.

The hypothesis of a metaphoric process as a part of the unconscious mind was introduced into psychoanalysis by Arnold Modell (1990) in his depiction of the analytic method for addressing emotional memories that unconsciously guide action. Modell has extended this hypothesis in more recent work (e.g., Modell, 1997, 2000, 2003, 2005, 2007), elucidating the key idea that emotional experience is unconsciously and involuntarily processed metaphorically. Dr. Modell has presented an elegant overview and expansion of his psychoanalytic contributions to the subject of metaphor in the introductory paper of this issue.

In his lucid article, “Metaphor—The Bridge Between Feelings and Knowledge,” Modell describes metaphor as an unconscious psychological process, as well as an expression of an as yet to be specified neurophysiological process that transfers meaning between dissimilar domains, and, through the use of novel recombinations, transforms meaning. As part of the unconscious mind, the metaphoric process is assumed to be a fundamental mode of cognition (with its own developmental line) central to the human imagination. Originating in bodily sensations and feelings and appropriated by language, metaphor represents an innate, continuous, lifelong capacity. Modell accordingly conceptualizes metaphor as a “pattern detector,” following cognitive linguist M. Lakoff and philosopher M. Johnson's work, and an “organizing template that establishes the categories of emotional memory,” extending neurobiologist G. Edelman's categorical theory of memory. The enduring connection of metaphor to bodily sensations, feelings, and categorical memory enables Modell to speak of metaphor as a biological property of mind and as a key to the development of a “neurobiology of meaning,” a rubric that anticipates a synthesis of the controversy between biologically oriented and hermeneutically oriented psychoanalysts.

Sandra Kiersky Ph.D. and James Fosshage Ph.D.

James Fosshage

James Fosshage  

Introduction

We want to thank each of the contributors to this issue for reminding us of our common ground as analysts, for highlighting our differences, and for sharing with us the unique perspectives that only they could have brought to this case. It is rare that we have the opportunity to read the detailed clinical process of a case conducted by a senior psychoanalyst and theorist. Anne Alvarez has given us both a rich and rare opportunity.

It's impossible to summarize fully the various positions we've collected here. Each is rich and complex. Despite this, we do want to say a few words about the discussions as a whole and what they suggest to us about the current state of psychoanalytic theory and clinical practice.

Certain issues remain central for our contributors, regardless of their specific point of view. These are beliefs in a dynamic unconscious and that transference and countertranference are at the heart of the psychoanalytic process. All the discussants have powerful commitments to a developmental point view and to the centrality of affects in development and in the analytic exchange. Even though conceptualizations of these phenomena vary, at times markedly so, these fundamentals tie our theorists together as analysts and define, in a general way, what we mean by psychoanalysis. Along this line, it was striking to see the influence of systems theory on everyone, despite the fact that not everyone embraces a nonlinear model of development.

Within these broad frames, however, the discussions contain very real theoretical differences that result, of course, in different clinical approaches. Many of these differences, we suggest, reflect a continuum of understanding Luisa's experience as largely shaped by internal forces or co-constructed in relational fields; linear versus nonlinear models of development; and interpreting rather than collaboratively elaborating a patient's subjective world.

Sander Abend's focus, for example, is primarily on internal conflicts generated in the inevitable clash between innate impulses and external prohibitions. Abend appears to stand firmly on the side of conflict as the great organizer of psychic life. From his perspective, Luisa is a conflicted young woman experiencing a resurgence of unresolved oedipal conflicts as she passes from childhood through adolescence to a sexual adult. These conflicts of a sexual and aggressive nature result in envy and competitive feelings toward her cool, maternal analyst. For Abend, it is the oedipal drama with its waxing and waning throughout life that stirs up trouble and needs to be focally addressed within the analytic situation.

Interlude: Living and Working in Two Worlds: The Psychoanalyst in the Office, and the Psychoanalyst as Forensic Expert in the Courtroom

Moisy Shopper M.D.

Moisy Shopper

Moisy Shopper  

Introduction

Many of the ordinary working rules and prerogatives of the psychoanalyst become invalid once forensic work is undertaken. Forensic evaluation and testimony have their own unique rules, pitfalls, and countertransference and transference problems. Yet it is Dr. Gunsberg's position that the trained psychoanalyst brings unique skills and perspective to the courtroom, albeit sometimes not received well by the Court. Despite the different perspectives, goals, and origins of psychoanalysis and the law, Gunsberg traces the historical roots of their mutual interaction. Collaboration by lawyers and psychoanalysts has lead to significant advances in legal doctrine in both criminal law and family law issues.

Gunsberg presents case material that demonstrates the value of the psychoanalytic perspective and training in preparing and defending the forensic evaluation. Forensic work, although intellectually both difficult and gratifying, can be very stressful, particularly when there is an intelligent, informed, and persistent cross-examination. In fact, advising an attorney on the cross-examination of experts and/or individuals is another use of psychoanalytic knowledge in the courtroom. Gunsberg concludes with a detailed discussion of the legal and psychoanalytic dilemmas concerning confidentiality. She also reminds us that the treating psychoanalyst and the psychoanalytic forensic evaluator must be two different people since their relationship to important issues such as confidentiality and factual reality is not the same.

Interlude: What I Learned From the Edenton “Little Rascals” Sex Abuse Trial

Linda Gunsberg Ph.D.

Linda Gunsberg

Linda Gunsberg  

Introduction

Dr. Shopper writes about his experience as a forensic psychiatric expert in the case of The State of North Carolina v. Robert F. Kelly, Jr. A giant in the field of psychoanalytically trained forensic experts, Dr. Shopper shares his shock primarily at the four mental health professionals who functioned as psychotherapists to the “traumatized” preschool children who attended the day-care center where alleged sexual abuse occurred at the hands of the husband of the day-care center owner. These psychotherapists planted created information into the psychotherapy sessions of the children and conducted the psychotherapy under the premise that these preschoolers had been sexually abused. They also, in their work with the parents of these preschoolers, stimulated parental regression, in that the parents' own sense of reality was suspended. Instead, the parents assumed the reality presented by the police interrogators and child therapists. When parents suspend their own reality testing, the parenting function suffers, since parents relinquish their own fantasy-reality distinctions and, as a result, cannot encourage the child to make his own reality–fantasy distinctions. Relying on a constructed reality by police officers and therapists allows for both children and parents to regress, and naively believe the distorted created reality of those taken in by mass hysteria. This process actually creates symptoms that did not previously exist. The ability to discriminate between these created symptoms and symptoms that honestly develop can be distinguished by the psychoanalytically trained expert.

Parental alienation, a process often seen in divorcing families, is similar to this, in that a child is encouraged, maybe even persuaded, to relinquish his own sense of reality, and adopt the “reality” of one parent and therefore turn against the other parent. Whether in a day-care center allegation of child abuse or a divorcing family, the vulnerable child is not treated as an individual with his own view, but rather is coerced by another person to relinquish his autonomous views and regress by having his views merge with those of others. The short- and long-term effects of such coercion and regression to an undifferentiated state on the development of these young children is yet to be studied. Will these children ever be able to return to psychotherapy at a later date? And, if they do, will it be without the feeling that the therapist will “play” with their minds?

What I Learned From the Edenton “Little Rascals” Sex Abuse Trial

Moisy Shopper M.D.

Moisy Shopper

Moisy Shopper   Moisy Shopper, M.D., is at St. Louis Psychoanalytic Institute where he is a Training and Supervising Analyst in both adult and child analysis. He is also clinical Professor of Child Psychiatry and Pediatrics, Emeritus, St. Louis University School of Medicine, St. Louis, MO.

During the late 1980s and early 1990s, allegations of sexual abuse and satanic sexual abuse ravaged child day-care centers, their directors, and their staff. Many were convicted and jailed. As the psychiatric expert for the defense in the Edenton, North Carolina “Little Rascals” trial, I had access to mountains of data. As a result of my total immersion in this case and several earlier ones, I came to appreciate the massive irrational effect that mass hysteria exerts on parents, children, and professionals. Even the judicial process was affected, to the extent that only years later was the defendant's conviction unequivocally reversed, citing several basic judicial errors.

Psychoanalytic concepts are extremely important in working within a maximum-security prison, and especially in some of the most extreme parts of this difficult environment. To be most effective and most empathic, one needs to be aware of the impact of the prison environment. Emotionally, there is a tendency to identify with the inmates, to fear their and one's own aggressive impulses, and to retaliate or punish for these impulses. Within the identification with these inmates, there is also recognition of the difficulties in their backgrounds and factors that contributed to their being in the penitentiary.

Ana-Maria Rizzuto M.D.

Ana-Maria Rizzuto

Ana-Maria Rizzuto  

Metaphoric processes and verbal metaphors in analysis are at the service of self-objectification and activation of past affective experiences in the context of the transference. The process of working through benefits from metaphorical processes capable of integrating in concise verbalizations and complex somatic and sensory experiences past and present dynamically analogical affective experiences while opening up new affective moments with the analyst. The elaboration of the metaphors facilitates psychic transformation and leads to new metaphorical versions of who the patient is in relation to his past and present, himself and others.

Metaphor: A Fascinating Philosophic Puzzle Piece With Neuro-Psychoanalytic (NP) Implications

Fred Levin M.D.

Fred Levin

Fred Levin   Fred Levin, M.D., is an Associate Professor of Clinical Psychiatry at Feinberg School of Medicine, Northwestern University, and a Training and Supervising Psychoanalyst at the Chicago and Minneapolis/St. Paul Institutes for Psychoanalysis. Fred is the author of Psyche and Brain (2003c, Madison, CT: International Universities Press) and Mapping the Mind (2003a: New York: Karnac Press).

In 1980 a number of scholars independently discovered methods for studying “aha” reactions, and the role of metaphorical language in human activities. I see my work as parallel to that of Lester Luborsky, Arnold Model, and Lakoff and Johnson, but with a special interest on my part in bridging psychological and biological perspectives. In my article, I review the history of my own voyage towards such bridging, portrayed in my books, Mapping the Mind (2003a) and Psyche and Brain (2003c), and papers tying together affect theory, learning theory, cognitive theory, and neuroscience insights on how emotion is instantiated in brain (and the role of the cerebellum). Basically, the idea is that mind makes brain makes mind makes brain—ad infinitum. Building on the work of Eric Kandel (on explicit memory) and Masao Ito (on implicit memory), we end up with new ways of understanding emotion and Freud's conscious/unconscious distinction.

The Clinical Power of Metaphoric Experience

Joseph Lichtenberg M.D.

Joseph Lichtenberg

Joseph Lichtenberg  

Introduction

Early in my career as a therapist, I inadvertently learned the power of metaphoric experience. I was a first-year resident in Spring Grove State Hospital and in charge of a closed ward of patients still considered “active” as compared to “chronic.” I decided to treat, that is, have regularly scheduled sessions with, one of the ward patients, a paranoid middle-aged woman who was the most continuously angry person I had ever seen. We would sit in my office with her pouring out a steady flow of venom at her husband, the nurses, and the hospital. I would listen, comment rarely, and occasionally ask a question when I thought she might possibly answer without being more upset. As she talked I would rock back and forth in my office chair. In retrospect, my rocking was a form of self-soothing that I was offering myself to enable me to be able to contain the poisonous affect she was pouring out. One day as I rocked I noted a sudden look of anxiety on her face. Intuitively, I assumed it had to do with my precarious chair movements. Spontaneously I said: “Don't worry, I won't fall. I'm an expert.” To my total surprise, she responded: “Oh, thank goodness. I've been so worried that I'd steal you from your wife.” As we each overcame our mutual startle, I noticed a change in her demeanor. Her face relaxed and her angry tone was replaced with a conversational exchange. On the ward, her tension-ridden intimidating behavior lessened and the nurses recommended extending her “privileges.” And although I was as yet too inexperienced to know how to apply it during our sessions, I now understood that infidelity was an important theme in her delusions.

Webster defines a metaphor as a figure of speech in which a word or phrase literally denoting one kind of object or idea is used in place of another to suggest likeness or analogy between them. In the “I won't fall” example, I did not intentionally use the phrase to suggest an analogy, but the patient recognized an analogy to a major theme troubling her. And then I too saw its metaphoric meaning. We had cocreated what I will call an emergent metaphoric experience.

Melvin Lansky M.D.

Melvin Lansky

Melvin Lansky  

Introduction

My concluding remarks will focus on some commonalities found in these very thoughtful and original psychoanalytic articles. Let me first note the extent to which the authors made use of great literary and religious texts. Wurmser draws from the Talmud, Dostoevsky, and Lagerkvist; LaFarge draws from Dickens; Buechler begins with some reflections on guilt and atonement on Yom Kippur; I cite passages from the Bible; and Rosen draws heavily on Dostoevsky, among others. A remarkable amount of the previous psychoanalytic literature on forgiveness has drawn from the insights of great works of literature (Lansky, 2001, 2003, 2005; Smith, 2002; Gottlieb, 2004; Schafer, 2005a, 2005b; Sprengnether, 2005). This utilization of great literary and religious works is by no means a gratuitous or dilettantish excursion into the world of applied psychoanalysis. These contributions are fundamentally psychoanalytic works, and ones with significant theoretical and clinical substance, not simply forays into psychoanalytic literary criticism. The usual brief clinical vignette that is used so often in psychoanalytic writing simply cannot capture the complexity of the contexts and natural history of situations in which forgiveness and atonement are usually found. We as psychoanalysts are not simply hermaneuticists and healers; we are also naturalists of the human predicament and of the viscissitudes of internal change. We psychoanalysts, as naturalists, have joined hands with great literary and religious writers, also naturalists, to gain an understanding of these complex aspects of the human predicament.

Each of the contributors to this volume stresses, in one way or another, the role of the superego or of deep identifications with the abuser. LaFarge is emphatic about distinguishing a superficial form of forgiveness that identifies with the part of the superego that does not permit manifestations of one's own aggression from the deeper identification with rageful, vengeful, and sadistic traits of the betrayer. My article emphasizes identification with the analyst as the vehicle for a change from destructive identifications with a critical and rejecting father to more accepting, benign identifications with the attitudes of analyst. Wurmser's article points to the centrality of the dictates of the superego in the problem of resentment and to the central role of benign identifications with a compassionate analyst in offsetting and replacing pathological identifications. Rosen's entire article is on the identification of the aggressor with the aggressed as driving into being the search for atonement. Buechler stresses the power of internalized professional standards, judgment from which, if standards are too severe, may drive regret into hiding, but allow for atonement and integration if they are more compassionate.

PROLOGUE

Melvin Lansky M.D.

Melvin Lansky

Melvin Lansky  

Introduction

The topic of forgiveness was absent in the psychoanalytic literature until the 21st century. Since 2001, however, a burgeoning body of work has appeared on the subject (Lansky, 2001, 2003, 2004, 2005, 2007; Akhtar, 2002; Smith, 2002; Cavell, 2003; Gottlieb, 2004; Siassi, 2004; Horwitz; 2005; Schafer, 2005a, 2005b; Sprengnether, 2005). Forgiveness and atonement are intimately related. Forgiveness involves the letting go of a claim of injustice and damage; and atonement, the seeking of forgiveness from the other, involves the seeking for release from the negative judgment of the conscience.

Perhaps the psychoanalytic exploration of forgiveness and atonement were so late arriving on the psychoanalytic scene because the topic tends to suggest something that is antithetical to the psychoanalytic attitude, the advocacy in moral or religious terms of forbearance from retribution in responses to injustice or injury, for example, the forgiveness of Joseph with his brothers or of Jesus on the cross It would be inimical to the psychoanalytic method to consider forgiveness or atonement to be basic psychoanalytic concepts, and even more problematic to regard them to be psychoanalytic values with the implication that one should forgive or shouldatone. I see such a view as allying with one aspect of conscience against the forces of aggression and disruption of social bonds in what often is a superficial resolution of a social conflict that is accomplished without deeper integration in the psyche (see also, LaFarge, this issue.)

Such a deeper resolution includes modification of the forces, unacknowledged or hidden shame often prominent among them, which drive resentful retributive states of mind into being. It is very much within the purview of psychoanalysis to view the problem of fixation to retributive states of mind as centered around a consideration of the cost of the bearing grudges and consequences of vehement retributive states in the case of enduring unforgiveness, and the cost of (not necessarily conscious) guilt if atonement—the receiving of forgiveness—is not attained. It may be costly, indeed, not to forgive if such forgiveness involves the resumption of cooperative involvements with, say, a presumed betraying ex-spouse over joint custody of children. Likewise, a failure to atone in response to one's guilt, conscious or unconscious, is not infrequently accompanied by conscious or unconscious punishment seeking or self sabotage. Forgiveness and atonement are areas of investigation to be understood by psychoanalytic investigation, not moral values or technical precepts within the field. We are, in this pursuit, naturalists, using our scientific method, not moralists.

DR. LAWRENCE FRIEDMAN

I shall begin with Lawrence Friedman's “Tractatus Metaphorico-Psychoanalyticus”—this playful takeoff on Wittgenstein is a remarkable tour-de-force. One imagines that Wittgenstein might have written this if he had been a psychoanalyst. This leads to a certain problem, as the voices of the philosopher and the psychoanalyst do not always coincide. Are we considering metaphor in the context of philosophic truth, in which logic plays a significant role, or are our views of metaphor derived from psychoanalytic observation? Friedman's contribution is enormously condensed and wide-ranging, including comments on the meaning of narrative and the extent to which the sense of agency includes moral responsibility. I have selected only a few sections for comment.

Wittgenstein's thinking about metaphor probably would not have been influenced by neurobiology, nor would he have necessarily believed that metaphor is embodied and is intimately connected to emotions and feelings. Friedman does not make any of these assumptions explicit, and his own position regarding the contributions of neurobiology and cognitive linguistics remains ambiguous. My first reading led me to think that Friedman does not share my basic assumption that metaphor is an embodied form of cognition that has a privileged relation to feelings. Yet, on further reflection I am not sure that we are in full disagreement on this issue. For, Friedman does believe that metaphor is a form of cognition as he begins with a discussion of category formation and the problem of comparison. If we retain the definition of metaphor as the transfer of meaning between dissimilar domains, there must be, of course, an implicit comparison of categories.

But then, in section 1.1 we read “all prediction is thus propaganda, urging the receiver to see ‘this’ as a ‘that.’” I was at first puzzled by the word propaganda. This sounds more like a philosopher speaking than a psychoanalyst. At the risk of sounding pedantic, I understand the term propaganda to mean a tendentious communication that alters our thoughts and beliefs. The term originally referred to the dissemination of religious belief. Propaganda attempts to undermine the agency of the self and negate independent judgment. But this is what we, as psychoanalysts, attribute to an unconscious process. Does Friedman (speaking as Wittgenstein) wish to avoid the term unconscious in this context? It is true that metaphor causes us to think “this” rather than “that,” but does Friedman believe, as I do, that what causes us to think “this” rather than “that” is an unconscious process? Discussion of Craige's “Terminating Without Fatality”

Joseph Schachter M.D. and Ph.D.

Joseph Schachter

Joseph Schachter   Joseph Schachter, M.D., Ph.D., is a member of the Columbia University Psychoanalytic Center for Training and Research. He is retired and living in New York City.

Craige's concept of termination and the related concept of post-termination contact are based on Freud's early, one-person model of analytic therapy as a medical treatment for the cure of a disease. Post-termination contact was considered appropriate only if the patient needed additional therapy. Subsequent development to a two-person model of treatment, which recognizes the critical importance of the patient–analyst relationship, requires modification both of concepts of termination and of post-termination contact. I propose that whether there should be such contact, and what it's nature should be, should be mutually decided by patient and analyst in the termination phase, based on their risk/benefit evaluation of such meetings. The intimate, loving patient–analyst relationship, which has enhanced the patient's development, should be able to continue in some form after the end of treatment unless substantial, unresolved problems of either patient or analyst proscribe such meetings.

Living and Working in Two Worlds: The Psychoanalyst in the Office, and the Psychoanalyst as Forensic Expert in the Courtroom

Linda Gunsberg Ph.D.

Linda Gunsberg

Linda Gunsberg   Linda Gunsberg is Chair of the Washington Square Institute Family Forensics Training Program in New York, a graduate of the New York University Postdoctoral Program in psychotherapy and psychoanalysis, and in private practice.

The responsibilities of the psychoanalyst who enters the courtroom as a forensic expert are different from those of the treating psychoanalyst. The public exposure of the psychoanalytic forensic expert's work in the courtroom often becomes grounds for attempts to denigrate and deflate the self-esteem and credibility of the forensic expert. Yet, the courtroom is an exciting arena for the application of psychoanalytic theory and concepts, and the psychoanalytic method. The author shows how psychoanalytic adult and child training actually enhance the success of both the forensic evaluation and Court testimony.

Voices for Psychologically Injured Children: Psychoanalytic Testimony During Civil Litigation Helps Bring Social Change, Settlements, and Jury Awards

Gilbert Kliman M.D.

Gilbert Kliman

Gilbert Kliman   Gilbert Kliman, M.D., is the Medical Director at The Children's Psychological Health Center, in San Francisco, CA.

Because of its depth and scope, child psychoanalytic testimony can make major contributions to the civil justice system. Attorneys can strategically use such testimony to favorably influence institutional practices and standards of children's care. When requested by a skilled attorney, carefully integrated with that attorney's professional tasks and skills, psychoanalytic testimony can lead to more thorough and knowledgeable compensation for injured children than occurs with superficial approaches to the course of psychological pathology and care. Governments and institutions are then likely to be required by courts and juries to pay appropriate, rather than token, compensation for negligently allowing children to be traumatized in life-damaging ways. The author draws on his experience in the field of psychoanalysis and forensic child psychiatry, in over 200 separate cases, most of them civil, many with multiple victims. About 70% were requested by child plaintiffs' attorneys, and 30% by defense attorneys. Despite important failures, such as in defense of a mother accused of the scientifically questionable condition called Munchausen syndrome by proxy, the cumulative impact of the psychoanalytic forensic endeavor helps increase beneficial social change. Child protection standards improve, and major compensation is given traumatized children when the negligent or abusive parties are held financially responsible. To show the measurable significance that the judicial system gives to psychoanalytically informed evaluations and testimony, the author draws upon plaintiff children's cases through 2001. Among these cases, his reports and testimony helped attorneys bring about awards and settlements totaling over a quarter billion dollars, when the non-profit project described ended.

Emotional Reactions to Forensic Work

Lycia Alexander-Guerra M.D.

Lycia Alexander-Guerra

Lycia Alexander-Guerra   Lycia Alexander-Guerra, M.D., received her psychoanalytic training at the New York Psychoanalytic Institute, and, subsequently, has studied Relational and Self Psychology, as well as Intersubjectivity. She is the current president of the Tampa Bay Institute for Psychoanalytic Studies, Inc., and the Tampa Bay Psychoanalytic Society, and the Co-chair of the Veterans Family Initiative. She is in private practice in psychoanalysis, psychotherapy, and psychiatry in Tampa.

The author of this article primarily functions, not as a forensic psychiatrist, but as a psychotherapist to patients at various stages of the legal process (as victims or their alleged perpetrators of crimes) who are referred by their attorneys. Complicating factors with regard to this kind of referral include: the censorship of material by the patient, whose psychoanalytic psychotherapist's notes may be reviewed by attorneys and the Court; the possiblity that the psychotherapist may have to be called to testify; and that the referring attorney lawyer may expect the psychoanalytic psychotherapist to “produce” a diagnosis which helps the patient's case. When “secondardy gain” is the primary motivation for forensic patients, the treatment often comes to an abrupt halt as soon as the trial is completed. The emotional reactions of the psychoanalytic psychotherapist may be heightened in such cases. Additionally, the treating therapist may oscillate between finding the crimes committed, and the patient who allegedly committed them, morally repulsive, and finding herself identifying with aspects of the patient victim/criminal. Two forensic cases are discussed, along with the author's personal moral and emotional reactions.

The Workings of Forgiveness: Charles Dickens and David Copperfield

Lucy LaFarge M.D.

Lucy LaFarge

Lucy LaFarge   Lucy LaFarge, M.D., is a Training and Supervising Analyst, Columbia University Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research; Clinical Associate Professor of Psychiatry, Weill Cornell Medical College, New York.

Psychoanalysts have often rejected the concept of forgiveness as unanalytic, but the capacity for forgiveness remains a quality that is valued by our patients and by society at large. Deeper forms of forgiveness require a reworking of the superego, recognition of the damage that injury has caused, and an accompanying process of self-forgiveness. Some injuries can never be entirely forgiven; with these, forgiveness is at best partial, and some elements of the injury are liable to be revived at times of anger and disappointment. The childhood of Charles Dickens was marked by an early experience of abuse and neglect, when his parents sent him, at age 12, to work in a blacking factory. Dickens later included a thinly disguised account of this experience in his autobiographical novel, David Copperfield. I explore the ideas about childhood trauma, and the way that it may be forgiven, that emerge in the novel and argue that the writing of the novel facilitated a process of partial forgiveness for Dickens, which deepened his work but left him vulnerable to the return of vengeful wishes in his later life.

Setting Up the Doll House: A Developmental Perspective on Termination

Alexandra Harrison M.D.

Alexandra Harrison

Alexandra Harrison   Alexandra Murray Harrision, M.D., is Training and Supervising Analyst in Child and Adult Psychoanalysis, Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute, and Assistant Clinical Professor in Psychiatry, Harvard Medical School.

This article considers the contribution that consideration of the moment-to-moment process in psychoanalysis can make to an understanding of termination. Information on moment-to-moment interactions related to termination is developed from videotape microanalysis of termination discussions—focusing on a child analysis, but including an example from an adult analysis—as viewed through the structure of a developmental model (Tronick's dyadic expansion of consciousness model) that is consistent with dynamic systems theory. The theory emphasizes the co-creation of meaning that occurs in an analysis, as indicated by verbal, as well as nonverbal, interactions that are apparent in the videotape. The insights from this approach can enrich the traditional psychoanalytic views on termination by emphasizing the ongoing developmental process, with termination more of an important step in this process than a specific ending.

The Centrality of Metaphor and Metonymy in Psychoanalytic Theory and Practice

Antal Borbely M.D.

Antal Borbely

Antal Borbely   Antal F. Borbely, M.D., is in private practice in New York City. His list of published works includes “Towards a temporal theory of the mind” (1987, Psychoanalysis and Contemporary Thought, 10(4): 459–487), “A psychoanalytic concept of metaphor” (1998, Int. J. Psycho-Analysis, 79(5): 923–936), and “Toward a psychodynamic understanding of metaphor and metonymy: Their role in awareness and defense” (2004, Metaphor and Symbol, 19: 91–114), and “Metaphor and psychoanalysis” (2008, in: R. Gibbs, Ed., The Cambridge Handbook of Metaphor and Thought, Cambridge: Cambridge University Press).

Psychoanalytic theory is recast by interpreting the main psychodynamic concepts transference, interpretation, and defense temporally, and thereby showing their greater-thanassumed connection. They are congruent with each other as temporal metaphors, differing only regarding the direction and scale of influence. Transference interprets the present from the past; psychoanalytic interpretation as well as ongoing self-interpretation interpret the past from the present; healthy defense, tantamount to insight, is a second-order metaphor, metaphorically articulates the interpretation of transference, two first-order temporal metaphors. The psychoanalytic setting engenders a paradoxical tension between the basic rule (no censuring of personal feelings towards the analyst) and the basic contract (no personal relationship with the analyst beyond being coinquirers). This is conducive to metaphorization of traumatically lost metaphoricity. Metaphor theory, by resolving structural theory contradictions, simplifies psychoanalytic theory (e.g. “defense is understood as the interpretation of transference”), rendering it meaningful and accessible to nonanalytic cognitive scientists.

On Becoming a British Psychoanalyst

Elizabeth Spillius Ph.D.

Elizabeth Spillius

Elizabeth Spillius   Elizabeth Spillius, Ph.D., is a Training and Supervising Analyst of the British Psychoanalytical Society.

This article describes a personal journey from social anthropology to psychoanalysis, first through training at the British Psychoanalytical Society from 1956 to 1964, then to becoming a Member and Training Analyst. I describe the development of a career involving the usual things a psychoanalyst is likely to do in addition to clinical practice: supervising students, participation in seminars and discussions with colleagues, teaching, writing, serving on various committees, being editor of a series of psychoanalytic books, and trips abroad to teach and to consult with colleagues about other points of view. This is the bare bones, but I also try to describe the development of some of my psychoanalytic views and attitudes, including a brief look at the British Society with an ex-anthropologist's eye.

The Atonement–Forgiveness Dyad: Identification With the Aggressed

Irwin Rosen Ph.D.

Irwin Rosen

Irwin Rosen   Irwin C. Rosen, Ph.D., is a Training and Supervising Analyst at the Greater Kansas City Psychoanalytic Institute. Prior to that, he was a Training Analyst and Director of the Adult Outpatient Department at the Menninger Clinic in Topeka, Kansas.

In an effort to assuage the dystonicities of guilt and anxiety, the atoner forms an identification with his victim. Such an identification is, for the most part, unconscious and, to follow Racker's categorization, is either a concordant or a complementary one, with each pattern generating a distinct atonement narrative. Atonement is synonymous with neither reparation nor guilt, although each of them contributes to its formation and vicissitudes.

Prominent in relational scenarios within the work of atonement is the search for a punitive “bad-enough object,” an external, self-recruited gratifier of the internal need for punishment. Later atonement scenarios are often thematically linked to earlier fantasies of destruction of the maternal breast (in Kleinian theory) or to the unfolding of the classical Oedipal tragedy.

Atonement and forgiveness are constructed between the people involved, rather than being granted by one or attained by the other. Atonement wishes shape a number of partial identificatory processes that, when activated, form the ambience of the atoner–forgiver dyad. These include elements of repair, reconciliation, and repentance.

The plotlines of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov reflect Dostoyevsky's emerging understanding of the atonement process, from an earlier focus on Raskolnikovian self-torment to an Alexian (Karamazov) vision of reparative benevolence. Revenge and atonement are closely linked, with atonement often representing revenge against the self, taken on behalf of a complementarily-identified-with victim. This article provides some clinical manifestations of atonement, representing a continuum of greater or lesser psychopathology.

Moving on From the Suburbs

Robin Anderson

Robin Anderson

Robin Anderson   Robin Anderson is a Training Analyst in adult, child, and adolescent analysis at the British Psychoanalytical Society and formerly Consultant in Adolescent Psychiatry at the Tavistock Clinic.

This is an account of my development as a psychoanalyst beginning in a safe but very unquestioning culture of a London suburb. Some unusual features of my childhood, as well as a natural curiosity, made me need to question the apparent certainties of my surroundings. I describe how a number of events—the death of my father, my illness as an adolescent, and an unlikely encounter with psychoanalysis shortly after, set me onto a rather slow road toward becoming a psychoanalyst several years later. I describe the influences that were important to me. I have always been most inspired by those who could explain complex ideas in a simple and straightforward way, and this has become important objective for me.

The psychoanalytic relationship is unique among intimate relationships, in that its ultimate goal is separation. After termination, the analysand mourns the loss of the analyst and while feeling vulnerable and bereft, faces demanding emotional tasks alone. The post-termination phase is a precarious time during which the hard-won gains of an analysis may be threatened or even lost. Given the analysand's vulnerability, it is disturbing that many of our common termination practices may undermine the patient's leave-taking and harm the positive internal images of the analyst and the analytic relationship that have been forged during the analysis. Findings from recent research about the patient's experience after analysis are presented and implications are drawn for practice regarding the termination and post-termination phases. The author recommends that our theory and technique of termination should be reexamined and revised in light of new research and within the context of contemporary two-person theories of psychoanalysis.

The Superego as Herald of Resentment

Léon Wurmser M.D. and Dr.Phil.HC.

Léon Wurmser

Léon Wurmser   Léon Wurmser, M.D., Dr.Phil.HC., is Supervising and Training Analyst, New York Freudian Society, Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, University of West Virginia.

Clinical work shows again and again what large role the affect of resentment (alias unforgiveness) plays in psychopathology. It is not a simple affect and can be recognized as one important way of trying to solve early and late conflicts, but one that leads to a constant renewal of such conflicts. It has therefore a peculiar and special relationship to repetition compulsion.

It is not only with patients that we encounter its intense and drive-like power of motivation, but we hit upon its presence in families and in social institutions. Political leaders owe their power of persuasion often, maybe mostly, to the skillful play on widespread and sometimes contradictory resentments; their own often palpably burning resentment may serve as a magnetically sensitive instrument resonating to the popular and multiply caused sense of resentment.

Furthermore, it was Nietzsche and Scheler who drew attention to the degree of resentment which animates the morality of the West, particularly that of Christianity. Antisemitism represents a particularly virulent form of resentment.

The connection of morality and resentment is also clinically confirmed over and over again. In our analytic work, we keep observing how the value judgments and the underlying value attitudes are many times permeated by a spirit of resentment. This may not only hold true for the patients themselves, but we often notice how a deep resentment has dictated the value feelings which were transmitted from generation to generation in the family and how it has dominated entire religious and ethnic communities.

In the inner life of the patients, this resentment shows itself in a double form: on the one side as a yelling inner voice of self-beratement and self-condemnation, on the other side in the enduring bitterness, in the simmering indignation that suddenly breaks out in impulsive actions and in defiance against the expected or perceived condemnation from without.

Till Death Do Us Part

George Moraitis M.D.

George Moraitis

George Moraitis   George Moraitis, M.D., is former training and supervising analyst, Chicago Institute of Psychoanalysis.

In this article, the termination of analysis is examined from the vantage point of the analyst. The nature of the bond that analysts form with their patients is explored, as well as the extent to which this bond interferes with their capacity to facilitate the process of terminating the analysis. Patients with severe psychopathology cannot be expected to terminate their analyses the same way neurotics do. Both analysts and patients must come to terms with their unrealistic expectations of themselves and of the healing powers of psychoanalysis in order to avoid an interminable and unproductive process.

James Fosshage and Sandra Hershberg

Sandra Hershberg

Sandra Hershberg  

Introduction

The last time that the psychoanalytic issue of “termination” served as a focus of study for a Psychoanalytic Inquiry issue was in 1982. A number of questions were addressed: (1) criteria for termination; (2) the process of termination; and (3) the subjective response to termination of analysand and analyst on those occasions when there is a sense of success as well as at those times when there is a sense of premature interruption.

Over the 25 years following this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry, we have witnessed and participated in the ongoing emergence of two psychoanalytic paradigm shifts: the first, objectivisim to constructivism and the second, intrapsychic to relational field theory. During the same period of time psychoanalysis has been in the process of integrating developments in infant and attachment research, cognitive psychology, and neuroscientific findings that have fundamentally altered our conceptualizations of psychological development, pathogenesis, transference, and therapeutic action.

We, thus, find it timely to revisit and to investigate the impact of these revolutionary changes in psychoanalytic thinking on the concept of termination and the clinical practice of analytic endings. Questions we wish to address include: (1) How do these paradigm changes in psychoanalysis affect our view of termination? (2) Does or should analysis end? (3) How does analysis end and how does it continue? (4) How do analysts and analysands negotiate endings and continuations? And (5) What is the experience like for each of the two participants, analysand and analyst? In keeping with our purpose and the tradition of Psychoanalytic Inquiry, we have invited a group of prominent authors who offer a range of psychoanalytic perspectives on our topic.

Subsequent to the studies of Stephen Firestein (1978) and Judith Viorst (1982), examining the psychological meanings of termination for psychoanalysts, Heather Craige (2002) and Lora Tessman (2003) have published two important research studies investigating the termination experiences of psychoanalytic candidates. We asked Heather Craige to lead off our project with a particular focus on the clinical implications of her research project. In turn, we have asked our group of authors to use Craige's conclusions as a springboard for their theoretical and clinical considerations on the topic of termination.

Jennifer Johns

Jennifer Johns   Dr. Jennifer Johns is a Member of the British Psychoanalytical Society and Chair of the Winnicott Trust.

I tell the story of my own development from the childhood of a psychiatrist's daughter in wartime Britain, through a brief career in family medicine, to the position of a member of the Independent tradition in British psychoanalysis. As well as having psychoanalysts from different theoretical orientations in my family, I became confused during my training by the different strands of thought and technique taught and promulgated in the British Psychoanalytical Society. For some time after qualification, I took the lonely path of listening mostly to my patients' material as the prime source of understanding mental suffering. It was only after a few years that I was satisfied at being able to connect psychoanalytic theory with what I heard in the consulting room, and following this was further able to explore different strands of psychoanalytic thinking to reach my own position.

The Analyst's Search for Atonement

Sandra Buechler Ph.D.

Sandra Buechler

Sandra Buechler   Sandra Buechler, Ph.D., is at the William Alanson White Institute.

Since an analytic hour presents infinite choices, it also provides infinite possibilities for retrospective regret. The analyst's work furnishes opportunities to regret acts of commission and omission. Missteps that seem like consequences of our personal character issues are likely to evoke shame and/or guilt, which can further complicate our feelings of regret. But genuine compassion and curiosity about ourselves can facilitate finding ways to atone. Atonement can be understood as a movement toward integration of all parts of oneself, or, more globally, a movement toward the inclusion of all human beings into the human community. For the analyst, atonement can mean becoming “at one” by finding a positive expression for what we have learned from our regrets. The challenge atonement poses is to face our shortcomings, yet retain self-respect and self love.

Arnold Modell  

Metaphor can be thought of as the currency of the emotional mind. It is now generally accepted that metaphor is fundamentally embodied and is not simply a figure of speech. We now know that metaphor is the expression of a yet to be determined neurophysiological process that has been secondarily coopted by language. I suggested that metaphor unconsciously categorizes emotional experience, establishing similarities and differences between the past and the present. In cases of trauma, the play of similarity and difference becomes constricted, and metaphor loses its capacity to create new emergent meanings. Finally, metaphor enables access to the unconscious and fosters empathic contact with the other.

Elizabeth Wolf

Elizabeth Wolf

Elizabeth Wolf   Elizabeth Wolf is a Member of the British Psychoanalytical Society.

Introduction

This issue is the fourth of Psychoanalytic Inquiry devoted to psychoanalysts exploring how they became the analysts they are today. The first focused on psychoanalysts trained in institutes of the American Psychoanalytic Association. The second was dedicated to psychoanalysts trained in institutes outside the American Psychoanalytic Association. The third was devoted to analysts in South America. This issue features psychoanalysts who have trained at the British Psychoanalytic Society and practice in Britain, though their country of origin may be outside of Britain. These four issues facilitate some comparison of the influence of geographical area and the contribution of societal and cultural differences to the analyst's identity and the analyst's approach to his or her patients. We also have the opportunity to compare and contrast different theoretical influences and learn more about differences (and similarities) in ways of becoming and being a psychoanalyst.

These articles also raise the issue of what it means to be a psychoanalyst at the start of the 21st century, a time of pluralism in the psychoanalytic world. Knowing more about how we form our analytic identities can, perhaps, help us to understand and better respect different ways of being a psychoanalyst. Can looking at the experiences of these six psychoanalysts, who trained in a society where pluralism existed, offer some insights for all into how we can exist together in the larger analytic world? It is Michael Parsons' theme, in his overview article, to explore and draw out the differences in the way British analysts have arrived at their sense of identity and some of the implications of this on creative exchange between the groups in Britain, which may have wider applications.

This issue offers much of interest not only to those wondering about what influences individually form an analytic identity, and how these six particular individuals arrived at who they are as analysts, but in depicting, albeit in an idiosyncratic and personal way, how the three groups in the British Psychoanalytic Society may have helped or hindered the development of psychoanalysis here in Britain. The British Society has long been esteemed for maintaining plurality. Here we have a snapshot of how well that worked for these individuals and what lessons or implications may be drawn for other societies that similarly face the challenges of diversity.

Introduction

Divorce is not known for bringing out the best in people. Sometimes it may seem to be more of an attack-and-destroy mission in which the prize is not a piece of land but the hearts, souls, and minds of the children involved. The “civilized divorce” rarely exists since few couples have been able to deal with their disappointments in the marriage: shattered dreams, hostilities, grief, and especially hatred. Hatred is often double-edged in that it is not only directed toward the spouse, but also toward oneself, although the latter is often subsumed and eclipsed by the former. The psychoanalytic forensic expert enters the minefield with the goal and hope of finding some clearing from which he or she can operate. It is almost inevitable that each party, recognizing the import and impact of the forensic expert's work, will feel endangered and attempt to convert the expert from a potential enemy into a secure ally. The appeal is not only to the forensic expert's reason, but also to his/her emotions. The forensic expert should hate whom he/she hates; and side with him/her. Rare is the divorcing party who puts the welfare of the children first and foremost, although many voice such altruistic sentiments. Each individual's parenting ability is sorely stressed and only a fraction of his or her ordinary capabilities.

To Demby, the term conflict does not adequately convey the emotional components as well as it emphasizes the cognitive aspects of divorce. Although conflict may be resolved to some degree and to some modicum of satisfaction to both parties, hatred is not so easily worked through since it contains both the attempt to separate and the desire to hold onto one's spouse. Yet it must be acknowledged as the crucial element in the divorce and one that can sabotage the most carefully constructed custody agreement, and lead to continual legal motions to modify the agreement. It is the parents' rage at one another, fueled by a sense of narcissistic injury, which usurps the parents' ability to think about the child's best interests and welfare. In brief, the parenting function has been substantially replaced or overwhelmed by parental hatred for one another.

Shall the Twain Meet? Metaphor, Dissociation, and Cooccurrence

Donnel Stern Ph.D.

Donnel Stern

Donnel Stern  

Even when trauma can be remembered, the memory does not infuse the present with vitality or emotionality, as other memories do. To become a vital part of experience, trauma must be linked with other current experiences. Such links are metaphorical, in the sense meant by Lakoff and Johnson (1999). In metaphor, the meaning of a memory is carried over or transferred to a present experience. When such transfer takes place, trauma can be reflected on, because it can now be seen against the background of another experience. Transfer is made possible by cooccurrence, or the simultaneous presence in one's mind of a memory and a present experience. Such cooccurrences are potential metaphors; they can be actualized or refused. Modell (2003) tells us that this kind of refusal, common among trauma sufferers, prevents traumatic experience from becoming part of “emotional categories.” I refer to the unconscious refusal to tap the potential of cooccurrence—the unconscious refusal to create metaphor—as dissociation. This view of dissociation, and its breaching, is illustrated by a clinical vignette.

Estelle Shane   Estelle Shane, Ph.D., is Training and Supervising Analyst, The Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis, Los Angeles, Training and Supervising Analyst, The New Center for Psychoanalysis, Los Angeles, and Faculty, Department of Psychiatry, University of California, Los Angeles.

Introduction

I'm happy to have been asked to be a part of this issue devoted to a consideration of the concept and process of the termination phase in psychoanalysis. I'm especially intrigued at the prospect of revisiting, with my respected colleagues, a topic that I, along with my coauthor, Morton Shane, had thought about and had researched in the psychoanalytic literature more than twenty years ago (Shane & Shane, 1984). The publication that emerged from our efforts contained a review of all of the literature on the termination phase published to date in psychoanalytic journals of interest to us, that is, journals related to the American Psychoanalytic Association and the International Psychoanalytic Association. A relatively complete review of articles concerning this subject was possible because, as Jody Davies (2005), reminds us, the idea of a termination phase was only invented by Edward Glover in his 1955 paper published in the Journal of the American Psychological Association, and it wasn't much talked about in the literature until the ‘70s. By the time my coauthor and I were researching termination in the late ‘70s and early ‘80s, however, it had already become a popular topic, though ideas about it were fairly uniform, at least in the literature we explored. In fact, the formulations on the ending phase of analysis were so narrow in scope that it was possible for us to organize in a rather short list all the criteria for initiating the termination process identified in these publications. These criteria included, most importantly, the resolution of the transference neurosis; the successful completion of the mourning process, including mourning the loss of the analyst; the ability to separate from and function apart from the analyst; and the development of a newfound or more adequately refined capacity for self-analysis. All of this signified, according to accepted lore, that the infantile strivings that had impeded the patient's development and that had then brought the patient into treatment had been relinquished, so that analysis could properly end. We ourselves had introduced our review paper on the topic by asserting our deeply held conviction, based on our reading of the literature and our own clinical experience, about the overriding psychoanalytic centrality of the termination process itself.

Steven Demby   Steven Demby, Ph.D., is in independent practice in New York City.

The concept of parental conflict, as it is used in the custody evaluation literature, rarely conveys the motivational complexity of chronic parental acrimony. The concept of pathological hatred better describes and explains why some parents continue bitter fighting years after their divorce. Kernberg's classificatory schema of pathological hatred is applied to high-conflict divorces in which such hatred may be viewed as an effort to destroy, while at the same time desperately needing, the other parent. Difficulties mourning the lost marital relationship, stemming from either character pathology or childhood trauma, create a fertile breeding ground for pathological hatred. The concept of parental competence is also frequently oversimplified in the custody evaluation literature, where it is viewed as an assortment of unrelated skills. From a psychoanalytic perspective, the capacity for parenting is viewed as an outgrowth of a parent's object relationships, defensive structure, ego functioning, superego functioning, and unresolved developmental conflicts. Pathological hatred of the other parent tends to erode the parent's capacity for nurturance, as the parent sacrifices support of the child's developmental needs to the goal of making the child a pawn in the interparental hatred. The negative impact on the child's development can be insidious. An understanding of pathological hatred in high-conflict divorce enables the forensic custody evaluator to assist courts in making appropriate recommendations for therapeutic intervention, as well as custodial and visitation plans that have the potential to ameliorate or at least contain the damaging impact of the interparent hostilities on the child's development.

Becoming and Being an Analyst in the British Psychoanalytical Society

Michael Parsons

Michael Parsons

Michael Parsons   Michael Parsons is a Training Analyst of the British Psychoanalytical Society and the author of The Dove That Returns, The Dove That Vanishes: Paradox and Creativity in Psychoanalysis (Routledge, 2000).

The articles of Elizabeth Spillius and Jennifer Johns exemplify contrasting ways in which an analyst may form her psychoanalytic identity. She may recognize and accept a particular theoretical standpoint as valid, and form an analytic identity around that position. Or she may engage with a variety of viewpoints, and form an analytic identity through the interaction between these and her own internal self-experience. These approaches coexist in the British Psychoanalytical Society. There has been the potential for creative discussion between them, especially as regards their implications for analytic training. These six articles together, however, reveal how hard it has been for such discussion to take place. Spillius describes the disparity between the Society's three groups in relation to candidates' choice of supervisors, and I discuss this further. It seems to reflect an underlying difference in approach to psychoanalytic training, based on these different views of how an analyst's identity is formed. I suggest that the difficulty in debating this freely reflects a fear that opening up the issue might lead the Society to split. In 2005 the so-called Gentlemen's Agreement, which for 60 years governed group balance in the British Society, was formally abolished. In the light of this, I consider what is needed for a Society creatively to contain divergent philosophies of training.

No matter what has come before, if the ending of the analytic relationship is not managed sensitively, much good may be undone. Analytic endings are emotionally challenging for analysts as well as patients. What was missing from the classical approach, at least as interpreted by Freud's American disciples, was appreciation of the personal relationship (Flank, 2006). In a relational view, the ending must be considered uniquely and mutually negotiated as part of a relationship that is both technical and personal. Accordingly, both permanent separation and separation with possible return are seen as just two of many possibilities for ending that the pair may co-create. Other options must also be considered.

Melvin Lansky M.D.

Melvin Lansky   Melvin R. Lansky, M.D., is a Training and Supervising Analyst, New Center for Psychoanalysis, Los Angeles, and a Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, UCLA Medical School.

This article presents a psychoanalytic formulation of forgiveness seen as the resolution of splitting underlying manifest and vehement retributive states of mind such as resentment, vengefulness, grudge, envy, bitterness, blame, and spite. Clinical examination suggests that these states of mind that are indicative of the presence of splitting are not always in ascendancy. They wax and wane in consciousness, depending on whether or not a shame-filled state of mind is present. Their appearance in consciousness is due to the instigatory role of shame before onlookers and the powerful role of hidden shame dynamics that do not always appear as overt shame. Examples illustrate a clinical impasse posed by the workings of intense splitting, the transformation of a shame experience into a dynamic of guilt in the firing of a very successful football coach after a disappointing defeat, and the working through of splitting in a patient pari passu with his increased bearability of shame. Working through of the splitting underlying the retributive emotions involves the increased bearability of shame, often with the help of an identification with the analyst. Vistas for future investigation include the role of the working through of resentment of the analyst in the analytic process and the relation of that resentment to instigating shame dynamics.

Much of the psychoanalytic literature on termination is steeped in ideals of autonomy, independence, and permanent cessation of contact. Although more recently some modified perspectives on termination have been offered, literature from various fields including contemporary psychoanalytic models, infancy research, and neuroscience supports a more extensive reconceptualization.
